The Hispanic Rise is here. And the next 25 years are ours to help shape!

What an incredible first day at the 2026 Hispanic Leadership Summit, organized by We Are All Human and The Hispanic Star in NYC!

Congratulations to Claudia Romo Edelman, Carolina Guardiola Romo, and the entire team for bringing together an extraordinary group of leaders to explore the economic power, influence, and future of our Latino community.

The message throughout the day was clear: Our collective power is undeniable, and the opportunity ahead is extraordinary. Now is the time to turn that power into action, investment, ownership, and lasting impact.

Some of the many key highlights that stood out:

✨ Latinos now contribute to $4.4 trillion to the U.S. economy representing the 4th-largest in the world if considered independently. 

✨ Investing in Latino progress and achieving spending parity could unlock an additional $322 billion in annual consumer spending, nearly $1 billion a day in economic opportunity.

✨ Our Latino dollar is estimated to circulate only once within our community; imagine the multiplier effect of intentionally buying from, hiring, and investing in one another.

✨ Latino entrepreneurs are among the fastest-growing business creators in the country, yet access to capital, networks, contracts, and operational expertise continues to limit the ability to scale.

✨ AI creates an opportunity to democratize access to knowledge while making it essential that Latino voices, experiences, and contributions are represented in the data shaping these technologies.

✨ Our stories of leadership, entrepreneurship, innovation, and achievement are critical to reshape perceptions and the positive narrative of our community.

It was incredibly heartwarming and empowering being surrounded by so many influential leaders, each bringing their expertise, perspectives, and commitment to making a difference.

It fills me with hope and excitement about what is possible. Change happens because people choose to lead, collaborate, challenge what is possible, and create opportunities for others. And when we bring those efforts together, we can continue shaping a stronger country and contributing to a better world for the generations that follow.

At UNITED LATINAS, we are proud to contribute to this movement by elevating Latina voices, amplifying their achievements and impact across industries, and building meaningful connections that create opportunities for leadership and growth.

We have the talent. We have the economic power. We have the influence. And we have an extraordinary opportunity to shape what comes next.

Here's to being intentional about the impact we create, the doors we open, and the future we build together!

Looking forward to Day 2! 💚

Sales candidates interview better than they did two years ago. I’m not sure they sell better.

Most candidates now prepare with AI. They know the company, the product, the competitors and the right sales terms. Their answers to standard questions are clean and well structured.

That makes standard questions less useful. “How would you approach a new territory in Germany?” gets a good answer from almost everyone.

So I ask less about what people know and more about what they did. I pick one deal from their CV and stay on it. Who was the first contact? Who else had to agree? Where did it get stuck, and for how long? What did you do next? What was the contract value in the end?

Someone who ran the deal answers these without effort. Someone who was on the edge of it, or prepared a story, runs out of detail after two or three questions.

For foreign companies hiring in Germany this matters more, because you often can’t judge the German-language part yourself. A candidate can be convincing in an English interview and still struggle in a German customer meeting. Have someone test that part in German, in a real scenario.

HR holds the most sensitive data in any company.
Salaries. Medical leave. Investigations. Social Security numbers. Disciplinary records.

Now imagine it pasted into a free chatbot.

It's already happening:

→ 57% of enterprise employees using AI admit entering confidential company data into public tools, and 68% use personal accounts instead of approved ones. (TELUS Digital, 2025)

→ 1 in 5 organizations had a breach tied to "shadow AI." Those breaches cost $670K more, and 65% exposed personal information. (IBM, 2025)

→ Only 37% of organizations have policies to manage AI or detect shadow AI. (IBM, 2025)

Banning AI doesn't work. People just use it anyway, out of sight. HR's job is to make the safe way the easy way.

8 ways HR can protect PII while working with AI:

1. Provide an approved tool. Use enterprise versions that don't train on your data. If you don't give people a safe tool, they'll bring their own.

2. Classify your data. Make it clear what is never allowed (SSNs, medical, investigations, pay records, I-9s), what must be anonymized, and what's safe.

3. Anonymize first. Strip names, IDs and unique details before asking AI to analyze anything. Small details combined can still identify someone.

4. Write a short, clear AI policy. One page people actually read beats twenty pages nobody opens.

5. Train everyone, including executives. Leaders are often the heaviest users of unapproved tools.

6. Vet your HR tech vendors. Ask where data is stored, how long it's kept, who can access it and whether it trains their models. Get it in the contract.

7. Keep a human in the loop. AI can draft, summarize and sort. It should not make hiring, discipline or termination decisions on its own.

8. Know the law. Illinois now requires notifying employees when AI is used in employment decisions, and more states are following. Check with counsel before deploying AI in HR decisions.

AI can make HR faster and smarter. But trust is HR's most valuable asset, and one careless paste can break it.

At Cisco Live Melbourne, Cisco announced it's adding Anthropic Claude Mythos to Cisco AI Defense for red teaming. In plain English, a frontier AI model plans the clever, multistep attacks a real adversary would try, then runs them against your own AI apps and agents so you can find the weak spots first.

Think of it like hiring a master burglar to test your locks. Except this one signs a contract, wears a name badge, and heads home the moment you say stop.

That's pretty much how the guardrails work:
✓ It only tests systems you own and have authorized
✓ Every test is tied to a named operator
✓ Any session can be stopped at any time
✓ Nobody can prompt it freely. It runs through a structured interface with a full audit trail

There's a second piece I love. Splunk is adding Tokenomics, which shows what each AI agent costs right next to how well it performs. Just over half of organizations say they can't control their AI costs today, so this one could matter a lot.

Cisco's Jeetu Patel put it perfectly: "You cannot scale what you cannot secure, govern, or observe."

Good to know: red teaming with Claude Mythos is coming soon for select enterprises, and Tokenomics opens in private preview in December.

My post last week about a recruiter interaction reached 5,006 people. My best post before that reached 111.

I reckon that's a signal y'all like this kind of content, so here's some more. 

This morning my job crawler found 3,531 open quality and R&D roles at 1,058 employers.

How it works:
• It reads employers' own hiring systems (Workday, Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, iCIMS, SuccessFactors) across about 10,000 career sites. That's roughly 500,000 postings a day, filtered to the 4,400 or so with quality or R&D titles.
• An AI model (Qwen) running locally on my MacBook in LM Studio reads each new posting and scores it against my resume. Degree and years-of-experience requirements are checked in code, so the AI can't wave them through.
• It runs itself every morning: about 30 minutes to crawl, an hour or so to score. Results go into a local database, and it builds a weekly market report from them.
• I built it in Python with an AI coding assistant. No paid job-board data.

Here's what the data says.

1. Industry sets your paycheck as much as your title does.
Pharma holds a third of the openings (1,178) and pays the most, a $193K median. Medical devices ($168K) and biologics ($163K) come next, then industrial ($148K). Food and supplements sit at $128K and contract manufacturing and testing at $118K. Pharma's median is 63% higher than contract manufacturing's.

2. Certifications get mentioned. They rarely get required.
Across 1,526 quality roles, Lean / Six Sigma shows up in about 1 in 5 postings, but only about 1 in 90 requires it. ASQ: named in 13.2%, required in 0.5%. PMP, PCQI and SQF Practitioner each appear in under 2%.

What employers ask for is experience doing the work: audits (57.5%), root cause analysis (31.9%), cGMP (30.9%), validation (28.6%) and CAPA (25.6%).

3. Remote is scarce.
Only 337 roles are remote, under 10% of the total, at a $173K median. California (545) and Massachusetts (419) each have more openings than every remote role combined. The Southeast has 343 roles and the lowest median, $129K.

4. What the charts don't show.
The typical posting asks for 5 years at Manager, 8 at Senior Manager, 10 at Director and 13 at VP. And roles move fast: postings that came down this week had been up a median of 20 days.


If you're searching, don't wait on a certificate or a remote listing. Pick your sector, go where the jobs are, and apply in the first week or two.

I saw it in billing, long before AI.

A correct calculation can still lead to a wrong decision.

Now AI does the math in seconds.
I started in AP, AR and billin. 
Then I moved to FP&A. 

Every number in a report started as someone's invoice, entry or guess.

Using a GameTideData example:
Say you ask AI to explain Q3 sales. 
If it only reads the invoices and finds invoiced sales up 18%, from $1,000,000 to $1,180,000. It suggests hiring 2 more sales reps.
The math is right.
But $140,000 of Q3 was one customer billed early for next year's contract.
Take it out and invoiced sales only grew 4%.

A correct calculation led to a wrong plan. 
The weak spot was an assumption. 
AI treated Q3 as a normal quarter.

Before you trust AI-built analysis, ask 3 questions:
1. Where did each number come from? 
A system, a person, or a guess.

2. What one-off is inside? 
One customer, one deal, one month.

3. What has to stay true for this to hold? 
Ask AI to list its assumptions, then check each one.

Where it breaks: these questions only find a weak assumption. 
Fixing it takes someone who knows the business.

Which of the 3 questions do you skip most?

Go build something.

Myth: You can fully automate employee onboarding with AI. 🚫

Why that’s misleading: onboarding includes dozens of small, repeatable tasks (collecting documents, creating accounts, sending welcome messages, answering common questions) that are perfect for automation — but it also includes high-trust, sensitive moments that must stay human. Offers, contracts and any action with legal consequences should be reviewed by a person. The first conversation with the hiring manager, the first-week check-in, and sensitive questions shouldn’t be handled solely by a bot.

Practical point: automate the checklist (document collection, accounts, FAQs) and build a clean handoff mechanism — a concise summary the human receives so the new employee never has to repeat themselves.

We spent twenty years teaching humans least-privilege access.
Now we have to teach agents the same lesson.

When an AI agent acts on behalf of a user, the instinct is to hand it the user's full access and let it work. That's exactly backwards. A person clicks carefully. An agent calls tools at machine speed, follows instructions from content it reads, and doesn't get a bad feeling before doing something irreversible.

The pattern that actually works in production looks a lot like the old security playbook, rebuilt for agents. The agent gets a scoped, short-lived token — exchanged for the user's token, narrowed to only the tools and data this task needs. Every tool call is authenticated. Every action is logged against the agent's identity, not lost inside a shared service account. And when the agent hits something outside its scope, it stops and asks — fail closed, not fail open.

The model gets the attention. The trust layer is what decides whether an agent survives its first week in a real enterprise.

AI has an ROI problem. 

Not because AI doesn’t create value.

Today we can measure what we spend on AI, but not what we get back.

IBM reports that 79% of executives see AI productivity gains, while only 29% can reliably measure ROI. [ibm.com]

We count licences, users, tokens, hours “saved” and pilots.
But that measures AI activity. Not business value.

I believe every significant AI investment needs an AI VALUE CONTRACT:

1️⃣ Baseline – What does the process cost today?
2️⃣ Outcome – What will AI improve: cost, speed, quality, revenue or risk?
3️⃣ Full Cost – Technology + data + integration + governance + change.
4️⃣ Evidence – What measurable outcome did we actually create?
5️⃣ Decision – After 90 days: Scale. Redesign. Stop.

If AI saves 30% of someone's time, that is not automatically 30% financial value.
It's capacity.

Value is created when that capacity becomes more output, lower cost, avoided hiring, higher quality or lower risk.

AI should be managed as an investment portfolio, not a collection of pilots.

The goal is not more AI.

It’s more value per euro invested in AI.

How are you measuring it?

The April 2026 CSM licensing redesign is being framed as a cost optimization exercise, but the deeper architectural consequence is a forced decoupling of feature access from customer identity. The new Foundation, Advanced, and Prime tiers are not just pricing tiers. They are a mandate that your service delivery flows must now be license-aware at the point of execution, not just at the point of contract.

The hidden trap is that the platform no longer enforces feature parity across your entire customer base. In the legacy model, if you had Standard licensing, the platform simply did not expose certain capabilities. Now, with the tier decoupling, the platform will let you run an AI-powered case deflection flow against any customer record. It is your instance design that must enforce that flow is only available to Prime-tier customers. The burden of governance has shifted entirely from ServiceNow's licensing engine to your architectural logic.

I have seen teams deploy a new proactive escalation flow across all customer segments, only to discover that their Advanced-tier customers were consuming AI capacity they had not purchased. The platform did not raise a warning. The architecture had no conditional routing that checked the customer's tier before executing the flow. The result was a licensing audit failure that could have been avoided with a single conditional flow step.

For hiring managers evaluating CSM expertise, the signal to look for is not familiarity with the new tier names. It is the ability to answer: how do you design a CSM instance where every flow, every AI skill, every premium feature is dynamically gated by the customer's license tier, without adding operational overhead for your agents? Someone who has built a reusable flow gateway that reads a customer tier field and routes execution accordingly, or designed a consumption dashboard that tracks feature usage against entitlement by segment, will outperform someone who can only describe the pricing changes.

The most effective CSM teams in 2026 are not the ones with the most advanced features. They are the ones whose architecture implicitly enforces that those features are only used by the customers who paid for them. If your team is adopting the new CSM tier structure, how are you ensuring your service delivery flows are license-aware without requiring manual oversight?

Recruiting is one of the hardest places to build a marketplace. Contrario (YC W25) seems to be making it work.

The model, as I understand it: startups post roles, a vetted network of 500+ expert recruiters and boutique agencies works them, and Contrario's AI handles the matching and admin in between. Recruiters get a steady pipeline of startup clients without doing their own sales. Startups get specialists without signing ten agency contracts.

The numbers they shared at launch in May: about $6M in annualized revenue in under 6 months, and $1M+ paid out to recruiters.

What I respect most is that they publish their marketplace data. Their November analysis says every forward deployed role startups brought to them was rated hard to fill, versus 63% of non-engineering roles. And it's about 18 days from meeting a hire to their first day. Most recruiting companies keep that data private.

What happens next:
1. Supply becomes the moat. One partner agency, MMC Search Partners, has generated $850K+ from 20+ placements on the platform since January. That story recruits the next 100 agencies better than outbound.
2. Their hiring data becomes the product. Founders will decide which roles to send, and how to run interviews, based on it.
3. The next lever may be client speed, not supply. Their own data says candidates a company says yes to within a day are more than 2x as likely to end up hired as those who wait three days or more.

ServiceNow stock has lost billions in market value.

But the bigger question isn't about the stock.

It's about the future of the entire ServiceNow ecosystem.

Let me explain.

On October 28, ServiceNow reported its Q3 results.

The numbers looked strong.

• $3.99B in subscription revenue.
• 21% year-over-year subscription growth.
• $13.65B in cRPO.
• AI contract value target raised to $1.7B.
• Agentic AI production consumption up more than 13x.

Yet the market wasn't impressed.

Why?

Because investors were looking beyond the quarter.

Q4 cRPO growth guidance came in at 18.5%, compared with 20.5% in Q3.

Then came another question:

What happens when AI agents start doing the work that enterprise software users currently pay for?

This is where things get interesting.

There are two competing narratives.

The first:

AI will disrupt traditional SaaS.

Fewer users may mean fewer software seats.

AI agents could automate implementation, configuration and support work.

The second:

Enterprise platforms become even more important.

Why?

Because companies still need:

• Governed workflows.
• Security and access controls.
• Audit trails.
• CMDB and asset intelligence.
• Enterprise integrations.
• Reliable systems of record.

AI can execute tasks.

But enterprises still need platforms that control what those agents can access, change and execute.

And that's a very different conversation.

Now, here's what I'm watching from the ServiceNow hiring market.

I believe the skills conversation will become increasingly important.

Not just traditional developers.

But professionals who understand:

AI and agentic workflow implementation.

ITOM, CMDB and enterprise architecture.

ServiceNow IRM and AI governance.

Platform integration and automation.

Security, identity and access management.

This isn't a prediction that every one of these roles will see immediate hiring growth.

It's a question of where enterprise investment and implementation priorities will move.

One thing is clear:

The ServiceNow ecosystem is entering an interesting phase.

The next winners may not simply be the people who know how to configure ServiceNow.

They may be the people who understand how to make enterprise AI work securely at scale.

My question to the ServiceNow community:

Do you believe AI will make ServiceNow less relevant?

Or will it make the platform even more important?

I'd like to hear from architects, practice heads, consultants and enterprise technology leaders.

As companies lock in 2027 budgets, a few hiring trends are becoming hard to ignore:

- Skills matter more than job titles. Employers are getting more specific about what people need to do—not just what roles they’ve held.
- Flexible staffing is becoming a planning tool. Contract, project-based, and fractional talent can help teams move forward while permanent headcount remains tight.
- AI literacy is becoming a baseline expectation. Companies aren’t only hiring technical AI specialists. They want people across recruiting, operations, sales, finance, and marketing who can use AI responsibly and effectively.
- Speed still matters, but quality matters more. A rushed hire can cost months of productivity. Strong screening, clear expectations, and better candidate experience are worth the extra effort.
- Retention starts before day one. Transparent job descriptions, realistic pay ranges, and honest conversations about flexibility are shaping offer acceptance and long-term retention.

The takeaway for employers: build a staffing plan that can bend without breaking. 

The takeaway for candidates: show what you can solve, not just where you’ve worked.

One of the most frustrating aspects of the labor market is how disconnected the unemployment rate can feel from the experience of looking for work. During my job search in 2025, I saw how difficult it could be to secure interviews and navigate lengthy hiring processes, even with relevant experience. That's why the term "low-hire, low-fire" resonates with me. Unemployment can remain relatively low while people who need jobs struggle to find them.

In a low-hire, low-fire market, employers are reluctant to hire, but overall job separations are also subdued. Employees may feel relatively secure in their positions, while job seekers face fewer openings and more competition. The unemployment rate alone doesn't tell us how long someone has been searching or how difficult it is to move into a new role.

The figures from early 2026 illustrate the mixed signals. Employers added 130,000 jobs in January, exceeding expectations, and unemployment fell to 4.3%. Yet revised data showed just 181,000 jobs created during all of 2025, and openings had fallen to 6.5 million by the end of December. A positive monthly report doesn't necessarily mean hiring has recovered.

Layoff announcements complicate the picture. Employers announced more than 100,000 job cuts in January, up 118% from a year earlier. UPS and Amazon announced plans to eliminate 30,000 and 16,000 positions, respectively. Meanwhile, employers announced plans to hire only 5,306 workers in Challenger's January survey, the lowest January figure since tracking began in 2009. These are announced plans, not a count of completed layoffs or total hires, but the contrast is striking.

What's interesting is that a difficult job market doesn't necessarily mean the broader economy is contracting. Economic output grew at an annualized 4.4% in the third quarter of 2025, even as employers cited restructuring, contract losses, and uncertainty as reasons to cut positions or delay hiring. AI is often mentioned, too, although its precise contribution is difficult to separate from other business decisions.

For people who are unemployed, fewer openings can mean months of applications and interviews with little progress. Employed professionals aren't unaffected, either. When opportunities are scarce, changing jobs or advancing a career becomes harder. I think we need to look beyond unemployment and consider job openings, hiring activity, layoffs, and time spent out of work. Having been through a difficult search myself, I know there's a difference between an economy that looks stable on paper and a labor market that gives people meaningful opportunities.

Is the "Product Manager" role now becoming obsolete? Here's why I think it is:

Week 7 at Nocturnal AI, and for the first time the team feels real.

After about 30 interviews, we’re now in contract conversations with the first people we want to bring on. They asked good questions. What exactly is my role? Who do I report to? How will I be reviewed? 

7 weeks in, a lot of those answers only existed in my head and Sarmad’s. So this week we wrote it all down. Our operating model. Our positioning. A defined role for every single hire. 

BUT, we are not hiring any product managers. That's where the forward deployed model comes in. 

Our engineers own their piece end to end. They sit with the client, understand the problem, build the fix and stay accountable for it. Nobody in between translating what the client meant. The person writing the code will be the person who heard the problem.

We said we’d document the whole journey. This week that meant documenting the company itself.

Week 7 done. We keep growing.
